reason: Grasses and sedges have unisexual (pistillate) spikelets. The examples are correct.
'Pollen in tetrads' describes how the pollen is grouped, not whether a tetrad is present. It needs a pollen-unit rule, not 'present'.
'Optical quality' is a generic parent term. The examples are really colour and hair cover (lepidote, villous), which have their own terms.
A septum can be complete or incomplete. The examples are correct.
Lobes can be fringed with spines or spinules. The examples are correct.
Veins can be pale. The examples describe vein colour.
The PATO term 'structure' is a generic term and does not mean 'connate'. Connate pappus elements are real, but they need a fusion or connation term.
Bracts can be fan-shaped (flabellate).
Peduncles can be pendent, for example in fruit. The examples are correct.
The 'neck' of a moss capsule is not the same as a sporangium base, and 'short' alone is vague. A rule would need to tell the capsule neck from the base and handle bare 'short'.
Pebbled or bumpy seed surfaces are common. The examples are correct.
Spathes can be papery (chartaceous).
Spathes can be glossy or shiny.
Heads (capitula) can be obconic.
Wrong reading. 'Compressed' means flattened, not 'condensed' (packed denser). A flattened-shape term is needed.
Capsules can be fusiform.
Flowers or buds can be ellipsoid (prolate). The examples are correct.
A spadix can be constricted between its sterile and fertile parts.
Internodes can be slender (grêle).
The examples are bare measurements with no part named. A rule would need the context word or the parent statement to say which part is measured.
Glands and surfaces can be smooth. The examples are correct.
A moss operculum can be hemispherical.
'Coherent' means that like organs stick together (anthers, pollen). 'Attachment quality' is generic. A rule would need the bearer and a more specific cohesion or fusion term.
'Retrorse' usually describes the direction of hairs or prickles on the pedicel, not the pedicel itself. A rule would need to tell hair direction from organ orientation.
Lobes and teeth can be filiform.
Phyllodes can be present or absent, so this is a presence statement. 'Phyllodial' on its own is a weaker reading.
Mericarp surfaces can be rough. The examples are correct.
Auricles can be round or orbicular.
Lobes and apices can be recurved.
A spadix or spadicle can be clavate.
Lobes can be reniform.
The examples mix a thick nutlet, a thickened ring and a neck. A rule would need to separate whole-nut thickness from a thickening on part of the nut.
An awn can be persistent or deciduous.
Sepals can be subcylindric.
Pseudobulbs and other organs can be oblong, including compound shapes like ovoid-oblong.
Pinnules and leaflets can be rhombic.
Lobes can be triangular-lanceolate.
Glumes can be deciduous or caducous.
'2-D shape' is a generic parent term. The examples have specific shapes (rhombic-hexagonal, polygonal, circular) that should map to specific terms.
Anther locules can be measured for length.
Involucral bracts can be deciduous.
Auricles can be conspicuous or obvious.
Pappus bristles can be filiform.
Pedicels can be cuneate (wedge-shaped), as the examples show.
Leaf margins can be fimbriate.
Pedicels can be flattened.
Leaf sheaths can be small or reduced. Some examples describe reduction to fibres, which is a different thing.
A stipe can be indistinct or inconspicuous.
A petal base can be auriculate.
A perianth can be subglobose.
Bulbil number can be counted, and bulbils can be absent or present.
Fronds can be fertile or sterile. Some examples add only a length, which is a separate statement.
An inflorescence axis such as a rachilla can disarticulate or not.
Axes and branches can be straight.
A lemma can be hispid.
The adaxial surface of a bract or phyllary can have its own colour.
A fruit pedicel can have its own colour.
An anther cap can be subglobose.
Veins can bear bristles, as the examples show.
Lobes can be rectangular.
